title: Hanuman makes himself small
hook: to comfort Sita, the monkey who just crossed an ocean calls himself the weakest of the army
carry: hanuman's humility: small self, big hope

segments.voice: Yesterday: her doubt. Even when Hanuman grew like a mountain, Sita said no, for safety, choice and Rama's honor. Your line: maryada: the right way matters, not just the rescue.
screen: `MARYADA: THE RIGHT WAY MATTERS, NOT JUST THE RESCUE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman has to leave Sita in the grove. She's chosen to wait for Rama. Goodbyes like this are the hardest part: you're leaving, they're staying, and you want to say something that lasts after you've gone. Before he goes, she gives him tokens to take back, and he gives her something too: his counsel. A few sentences meant to hold her up until help arrives.
screen: `THE HARDEST PART IS THE GOODBYE.` → `TOKENS FOR RAMA.` → `COUNSEL FOR SITA.`

segments.voice: First, Sita's tokens. She tells Hanuman a private memory only Rama would know. One day at Chitrakuta a crow kept attacking her, and Rama, angry, sent a single blade of grass after it, charged with divine power; the crow found no shelter anywhere until it came back and fell at Rama's feet. Then she unties a jewel from her hair, the chudamani, and gives it to him. And she says plainly that she can hold on only for a month. Then Hanuman counsels her. Don't grieve. Rama and Lakshmana will come soon with Sugriva's army. And because Sita has asked how monkeys could ever cross this ocean, he adds something surprising. There are many in Sugriva's army stronger than me, and none weaker. If I could cross, how much more easily can they? The monkey who leapt a hundred yojanas calls himself the least of the army. If he's the strongest, the rescue hangs on one monkey. If he's the weakest, help is enormous, and coming. He makes himself small, so her hope can be large. This is the Hanuman devotees love most: the strongest one in the story, and the humblest. In Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, when Rama later praises him, Hanuman says it was all Rama's power, none of his own. In Hindu devotion, humility means getting the ego out of the way so something bigger can come through. And it's one reason many families read this book, the Sundara Kanda, aloud when someone is sick or in trouble: it's the book where hope comes back.
screen: `THE CROW AND THE BLADE OF GRASS.` · `THE JEWEL FROM HER HAIR.` · `NONE IN THE ARMY IS WEAKER THAN ME.` · then, large: `SMALL SELF, BIG HOPE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, hold in mind someone waiting on something hard, a diagnosis, a result, a return, and say Hanuman's name or a short prayer for them, the way families read the Sundara Kanda for someone in trouble. If you don't pray, hold them in mind and let a few simple, true words of comfort form, shaped to what they most fear, not to what makes you look good. Breathe them slowly in and out.
Hanuman's counsel. His words to Sita before leaving: don't grieve, Rama will come, and there are many in the army stronger than me, and none weaker.
Your line: hanuman's humility: small self, big hope. Tomorrow, the strong one stops to think. Day six hundred twenty-four, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindu families read the Sundara Kanda aloud in times of illness or trouble, and devotees love Hanuman as both the strongest and the humblest of Rama's servants; the chudamani is a familiar image in Ramayana art.

Chitrakuta.meaning: the forest mountain where Rama and Sita once lived

chudamani.meaning: a crest jewel worn in the hair

Simhika.meaning: a sea demon who seized creatures by their shadows

yojanas.meaning: an old Indian measure of distance, many miles each

Sundara Kanda.meaning: the fifth book of the Ramayana, Hanuman's journey to Lanka

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 38 (the crow at Chitrakuta; the chudamani; one month)
Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 39 (Hanuman reassures Sita; none weaker than me)
Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Sundara Kanda (Hanuman tells Rama it was all Rama's power, none his own)

notes: Crow story details: the crow is identified in some tellings as Indra's son (Jayanta / Kakasura); the script avoids naming him and omits the loss of the crow's eye. Confirm.
Sita's 'one month' (that she will live only a month more): confirm Sundara 38.
Hanuman's statement that there are many stronger and none weaker than him in Sugriva's army: confirm (Sundara 39).

Title note: 'Hanuman's counsel' is read here as his counsel to Sita (day 624) and his own counsel with himself (day 625); his counsel to Ravana (Sundara 51) falls in 'the fight' (day 627). A Keeper may prefer a different split.
